Q1: Dispatch Call A (Maple St). Chest pain at 7.8 is a potentially life-threatening medical emergency and the highest-scored call the medic unit can handle. Holding a unit for a 9.0 threshold is a failure; the alarm activation at 4.1 is almost certainly a false alarm and the twisted ankle is far less time-critical.
Q2: Dispatch Call A (Pine Rd). A kitchen fire at 8.4 outscores the dumpster fire at 7.9 and a structure fire has the greatest escalation potential even with the family evacuated. Neither call reaches the critical threshold, so normal dispatch protocol applies: send the unit to the highest score.
Q3: Dispatch Call A (1st St). A reported person trapped on the 3rd floor with smoke showing is a rescue situation and outscores the elevator rescue 8.9 to 8.8. Ladder's primary mission is rescue from height, and trapped-in-fire carries a far steeper mortality curve than two people stuck in a stopped elevator.
Q4: Dispatch Call A (Hill Rd). The conscious diabetic emergency at 7.1 is a genuine medical call well within a BLS unit's scope. A BLS standby for an event at 5.5 is explicitly a standby, not an active emergency, so the unit goes to the real patient.
Q5: Dispatch Call A (River St). The scores are nearly tied, but breathing difficulty at 8.1 outscores the hip fracture at 8.0 and respiratory distress can deteriorate to arrest in minutes, while a fall with a hip injury is serious but typically stable. Tie-break by higher score plus steeper deterioration risk.
Q6: Dispatch Call A (Main St). The vehicle fire at 6.8 outscores the brush fire at 6.5, so it gets the available engine. Since mutual aid was offered, request it for the brush fire near homes so the property-exposure threat is covered in parallel instead of queueing behind the vehicle fire.
Q7: Dispatch Call A (Park Ave). A multi-vehicle accident with injuries at 7.5 needs command oversight, which is exactly what a battalion chief provides, and it is the only call in the queue. Holding a command unit idle with an active multi-patient scene waiting is unjustifiable.
Q8: Dispatch Call A (Cedar Ln). Stroke at 8.7 is both the highest score and explicitly time-critical with a treatment window closing, far outscoring the abdominal pain at 7.3. Delay here costs brain function by the minute; the abdominal pain call waits for the next available unit.
Q9: Dispatch Call A (Summit Dr). It is the only call in the queue and an empty queue with an idle unit is a failure, not prudence. A gas leak in an evacuated home still needs an engine on scene for hazard control, so send the unit now.
